edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Caeterum Baptismum non temere credendum esse sciunt, quorum officium est. Omni petenti te dato, suum habet titulum perinde ad eleemosynam pertinentem. Imo illud potius perspiciendum: Nolite dare sanctum canibus, et porcis projicere margaritas vestras, et manus ne facile imposueris, ne participes aliena delicta. Si Philippus tam facile tinxit eunuchum, recogitemus manifestam et exsertam dignationem Domini intercessisse. Spiritus Philippo praeceperat in eam viam praetendere; spado et ipse inventus est non otiosus, nec qui subito tingui concupisceret: sed ad templum orandi gratia profectus Scripturae divinae impressus. Sic oportebat deprendi, cui ultro Deus Apostolum miserat, ad quem rursus Spiritus, ut se curriculo eunuchi adjungeret, jussit, Scriptura ipsius fidei occurrit in tempore, exhortatus assumitur, Dominus ostenditur, fides non moratur, aqua non exspectatur, Apostolus perfecto negotio eripitur. Sed et Paulus revera cito tinctus est. Cito enim cognoverat Simon hospes vas eum esse electionis constitutum. Dei dignatio suas praemittit praerogativas; omnis petitio et decipere et decipi potest. Itaque pro cujusque personae conditione ac dispositione, etiam aetate cunctatio Baptismi utilior est: praecipue tamen circa parvulos. Quid enim necesse est, sponsores etiam periculo ingeri? quia et ipsi per mortalitatem destituere promissiones suas possunt, et proventu malae indolis falli. Ait quidem Dominus: Nolite illos prohibere ad me venire. Veniant ergo dum adolescunt, veniant dum discunt, dum quo veniant, docentur; fiant Christiani, cum Christum nosse potuerint. Quid festinat innocens aetas ad remissionem peccatorum? Cautius agetur in saecularibus, ut cui substantia terrena non creditur, divina credatur; norint petere salutem, ut petenti dedisse videaris. Non minore de caussa innupti quoque procrastinandi, in quibus tentatio praeparata est tam virginibus per maturitatem, quam viduis per vagationem, donec aut nubant, aut continentiae corroborentur. Si qui pondus intelligant Baptismi, magis timebunt consecutionem quam dilationem: fides integra secura est de salute.
thought_title: Baptism Should Not Be Taken Lightly
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, those whose duty it is know that Baptism is not to be believed in rashly. To every petitioner, you give your own, having a title likewise pertaining to almsgiving. Indeed, that is rather to be perceived: Do not give holy things to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine, and do not impose your hands easily, lest you become a participant in alien sins. If Philip baptized the eunuch so easily, let us consider that the manifest and evident dignity of the Lord intervened. The Spirit had commanded Philip to go on that road; the eunuch himself was found not to be idle, nor one who suddenly desired to be baptized: but he had set out to the temple for the sake of praying, impressed by the divine Scripture. Thus it was necessary for him to be caught, to whom God had sent the Apostle of his own accord, to whom again the Spirit commanded to join himself to the eunuch's chariot, the Scripture of his faith occurred in time, having been exhorted he is taken, the Lord is shown, faith is not delayed, water is not awaited, the Apostle is snatched away with the business completed. But also Paul was indeed baptized quickly. For he had quickly recognized that Simon his host was a vessel of election constituted by God. The dignity of God sends its prerogatives before; every petition can both deceive and be deceived. And so, according to the condition and disposition of each person, even their age, delay of Baptism is more useful: especially, however, around little children. For what is the need to also impose danger on sponsors? Because they themselves can also fail their promises through mortality, and be deceived by the outcome of a bad disposition. The Lord says: Do not prohibit them from coming to me. Let them come, therefore, while they are growing up, let them come while they are learning, while they are being taught why they come; let them become Christians when they can know Christ. What is the hurry for innocent age to come to the remission of sins? It will be acted more cautiously in worldly matters, so that to whom earthly substance is not entrusted, divine things may be entrusted; let them know how to seek salvation, so that to the one seeking, you may seem to have given. Not for a lesser reason, the unmarried are also to be postponed, in whom temptation is prepared both for virgins through maturity and for widows through wandering, until they either marry or are strengthened in continence. If anyone understands the weight of Baptism, they will fear the consequence more than the delay: intact faith is secure concerning salvation.

rejected: Do not give sacred things to dogs

bible_refs.note: Nolite illos prohibere ad me venire

pass_b_english: People whose job this is know better than to treat baptism as something you take on faithlessly. Handing it to every single person who asks turns the rite into a charity receipt — your own title, same as almsgiving. No, the real rule is the one Jesus gave: don't throw holy things to dogs, don't toss pearls before pigs, don't lay hands on anyone lightly, or you'll end up sharing the guilt of their sins. (Matthew 7:6) You want to cite Philip and the eunuch as proof that speed is fine? Look closer. The Lord's own dignity stepped in, plain and unmistakable. The Spirit ordered Philip onto that road; the eunuch wasn't drifting — he had gone up to Jerusalem to worship, already gripped by Scripture. God sent an apostle to him unasked; the Spirit told Philip to catch the chariot; the passage he was reading hit home at the exact moment; he was urged on, seized the Lord, believed without delay, didn't wait for water, and Philip was snatched away the instant the work was done. That's not a precedent for haste — it's a miracle. Paul's quick baptism? Same thing. His host Simon recognized him instantly as God's chosen vessel. God's dignity fronts its own privileges; every request can deceive and be deceived. So the delay of baptism fits each person's condition, disposition, even age — especially with children. Why risk sponsors? They can die and break their promises, or be fooled by a child's bad turn. The Lord says, 'Don't stop them from coming to me.' (Matthew 19:14) Fine — let them come while they grow, while they learn, while they're taught what they're coming for; let them become Christians when they can actually know Christ. What's the rush to send an innocent age to the remission of sins? You're more careful with worldly goods — you don't trust earthly substance to someone until they prove they can handle it; do the same with divine things. Let them learn to seek salvation, so that when they ask, you've actually given them something. The same logic holds for the unmarried: temptation waits for virgins in maturity and widows in loneliness, until they either marry or grow steady in continence. Anyone who grasps the weight of baptism fears the consequence more than the delay; intact faith is already safe for salvation.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful formal translation, and Pass B provides a fluent, idiomatic rendering that preserves all theological distinctions and causal relations. Scripture citations (Matthew 7:6 and Matthew 19:14) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant clauses. The title 'Baptism Should Not Be Taken Lightly' accurately reflects the thought of the chapter.
